author: A Robot
objectives: Explain the mechanics of apparent retrograde motion from both geocentric and heliocentric perspectives.
Compare the retrograde loops of different outer planets.
Predict planetary configurations that lead to retrograde motion.

modules.description: Observe Mars's apparent retrograde motion from Earth.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Describe the apparent path of Mars, including eastward drift and the westward loop.
instructions: Watch the red point of Mars as it moves against the background stars.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars moves along its eastward path, leaving a trail to show its progress.
clips.narration: We begin on Earth, looking at Mars. Over months, it drifts eastward against the constellations. Why does it ever stop and head backward?

clips.changeMeaning: Mars changes position to represent the retrograde loop.
clips.narration: Suddenly, it halts and reverses westward. This loop is the central puzzle of ancient astronomy.

modules.description: Explore the geocentric explanation using epicycles.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Contrast geocentric and heliocentric explanations and articulate why the heliocentric model is preferred.
instructions: Observe the mechanical nature of the epicycle orbit.

clips.changeMeaning: Mars follows a small circular path (epicycle) while orbiting the Earth.
clips.narration: The geocentric model used epicycles—small circles—to explain the loop. It works, but it's complex and requires arbitrary tuning.

modules.description: Understand retrograde motion via the heliocentric model.
modules.author: A Robot
educationalObjectives: Explain why retrograde motion occurs as a consequence of Earth overtaking an outer planet.
instructions: Watch as Earth swings past Mars.

clips.changeMeaning: Earth and Mars orbit the Sun at different speeds.
clips.narration: From space, the mystery vanishes. Earth simply overtakes Mars on an inner, faster track. No epicycles needed.

clips.changeMeaning: A line of sight is drawn connecting Earth, Mars, and the stars.
clips.narration: When Earth overtakes Mars, our line of sight shifts backward, creating the loop. It is a geometric illusion.
